How We Cut Our Build Times in Half

By Jane Doe · March 14, 2026

For most of last year our continuous integration pipeline was the slowest part of shipping a change. A typical pull request waited more than twenty minutes for a green build, and engineers had started batching unrelated changes together just to avoid the wait. This post describes the three changes that brought the median build down from twenty-two minutes to just under eleven.

1. Cache what is expensive to rebuild

The first and largest win came from caching dependency installation and compiled artifacts between runs. We keyed the cache on the lock file hash, so a cache entry is reused until dependencies actually change. Restoring the cache takes about forty seconds, while a cold install used to take more than six minutes.

2. Run independent jobs in parallel

Our test suite had grown into a single sequential job. Splitting it into four shards that run on separate machines reduced wall-clock time dramatically. We balance the shards by historical test duration rather than by file count, which keeps every shard finishing within a minute of the others.

  • Unit tests: four shards
  • Integration tests: two shards
  • Linting and type checks: one job

3. Profile before optimizing

Finally, we profiled the remaining steps instead of guessing. Two surprisingly slow steps were a container image pull that could be avoided entirely and a documentation build that only needs to run on the main branch. Removing those from the pull request pipeline saved another two minutes per run.

If you want to learn more, read our deep dive on CI caching or the sharding documentation.
